description_full: Community Healthcare Trust Incorporated is a real estate investment trust that focuses on owning income-producing real estate properties associated primarily with the delivery of outpatient healthcare services in our target sub-markets throughout the United States. As of June 30, 2026, the Company had investments of approximately 1.2 billion dollars in 197 real estate properties (including one property with sales-type leases). The properties are in 36 states, totaling approximately 4.5 million square feet in the aggregate. Community Healthcare Trust was established on march 28, 2014 and is based in Franklin, United States.
ceo_bio: Mr. David H. Dupuy | CEO, President & Director | Age 56 | Compensation: $1.3M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 35 people. Revenue per employee of $3.5M ranks in the above the sector median among Real Estate peers, improving at 30%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $1.0M of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $294K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 0× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Community Healthcare Trust Inco is a small-cap real estate business with a $423M market cap on $121M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +30% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +2.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $36M in free cash flow — roughly 30 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 11.06× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 12.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.2× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 12.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 6.4% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.6) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Payout ratio looks stretched — the dividend’s own margin of safety is thin
Carries more leverage than most Real Estate peers — a smaller cushion for the inevitable bad year
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sector_tailwinds: Trading at a 53% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Market is pricing in lower growth than the company has historically delivered
Valued at a 27% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Insiders are net buyers (100% buy ratio) — insiders sell for many reasons but buy for only one
10 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Real Estate sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 23% below the high.

The 4 covering analysts target $16.50 on average, 12% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 0.9% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.14).
It converts 30% of revenue into free cash flow, or 21% after stock compensation.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 30%.

hlth: Leverage is heavy at 12.1x net debt to EBITDA ($3.3M of cash against $532.2M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.2x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.57 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.5% over 3 years, 9.9% over 5 years and 30.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 149%).
Free cash flow has compounded -2.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 3.1% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (16.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 31, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 6.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 82%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (2 purchases, net $273K bought).
It returns 12.7% a year to shareholders (12.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 2.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.

people: With about 35 employees, each generates about $3.5M of revenue, 1.5x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 30.2% a year.
